items.prompt: Two clerks copy the same order total of $80. One writes $95, then the other writes $92. Which number does the sheet end with?
choices: $92, because the later write overwrites the earlier one
$95, because the first clerk's write is locked in and wins
$107, because the sheet adds both changes
items.explanation: The later write simply replaces the earlier number, even though it started from the same old $80.

items.prompt: What is a lost update?
choices: A write that failed and was reported as an error
A row that was deleted by a cleanup job
A change erased by a later write that started from old data
items.explanation: Both writes were based on the same old value, so the later save silently wiped the earlier change.

items.prompt: What does a database transaction guarantee about one write?
choices: It checks every business rule you have
It fully happens or it fully fails
It always runs before any other write
items.explanation: Atomicity is about all-or-nothing, not about your domain rules.

items.prompt: Is a transaction around each write enough to enforce 'total never above $100'?
choices: No, it does not know that rule exists
Yes, because each write is atomic and so always safe
Yes, if the database is fast enough
items.explanation: A transaction protects atomicity; the combined rule must be enforced by your own code.

items.prompt: In the clerk story, why did each clerk think their result was fine?
choices: Each had checked the other clerk's work first
Each was shown the final total before saving
Each only compared their own new total with the limit
items.explanation: Both read $80, so each $95 and $92 looked legal when viewed alone.

items.prompt: Which of these is an invariant?
choices: The order was created on a Tuesday afternoon by a clerk
An order's total never exceeds its credit limit
The warehouse prints labels in blue ink
items.explanation: An invariant is a rule that must hold after every change.

items.prompt: What was missing in the two-clerk story?
choices: One place that checks the rule on every change
A faster database that finishes both writes sooner
A bigger order sheet with more space for items
items.explanation: The rule 'total at most $100' had no single owner that checked it.

items.prompt: True or false: both writes in the story broke a database constraint.
choices: True, the database rejected the second write
True, the database lost the first write on purpose
False, both were valid writes that disagreed about their start
items.explanation: That is what makes the bug hard to see: nothing technically failed.

items.prompt: Services A and B each add an item to order #4471 inside their own committed transaction. The saved total is $92 but the items add up to $107. What is the root cause?
choices: Nothing owns the rule that items, total and limit stay consistent together
The transactions were not atomic, so half of each write was lost during the overlap
The database was too slow to finish the first write in time
The credit limit was set too low for orders of this size
items.explanation: Each transaction was valid alone, but no code checked the combined facts against the limit as one unit.
items.reference:
Two valid writes, one wrong result
A reads $80, writes $95
B reads $80, writes $92 over A
items on the order add up to $107, limit is $100
each transaction was atomic; the combined rule had no owner
Why: a transaction makes one write all-or-nothing; only your own modeled rule can say which facts must stay true together.
items.learnMore:
Atomic is not the same as consistent

Atomicity says a single write fully happens or not at all. Consistency in the business sense means the facts that belong together still obey the rules after the write. The database cannot know your rules unless something in your design names them.

Common mistake

Assuming 'it ran in a transaction' means 'the data is correct'. A lost update is made of perfectly valid transactions.
items.reflection: Think of two people editing a shared document or spreadsheet at once. What would tell the second person that their copy is out of date before they save?

items.prompt: A teammate proposes raising the database isolation level and calling the problem solved. What is the best response?
choices: It makes the credit limit rule unnecessary because reads are exact
It cannot help, because isolation levels never affect concurrent writes
Isolation levels are never relevant to concurrent writes at all
It may stop this overwrite, but the rule still has no owner for other cases
items.explanation: Isolation is a mechanism; the domain rule that facts belong together still needs a modeled owner.

items.prompt: Two writes both succeeded and both looked valid from their own starting point. Which description of the failure is most accurate?
choices: A deadlock, because each write waited for the other one to finish
A phantom read, because new rows appeared during the first read
A lost update, because each write was based on an out-of-date copy
A dirty read, because one write exposed uncommitted data to the other
items.explanation: Neither write was invalid on its own; they were computed from the same stale value.

items.prompt: What is an aggregate in domain-driven design?
choices: A table in the database with many columns and indexes on them
A service that runs on its own server
A cluster of objects treated as one consistency unit
items.explanation: It groups the objects whose rules must be checked together.

items.prompt: What is the aggregate root?
choices: The first row stored in the database
The one object outside code is allowed to call
The newest object created inside the cluster
items.explanation: All changes go through the root, which checks the rules.

items.prompt: Where should 'total at most the limit' be checked?
choices: Inside the root, on every change
Only once, in a nightly report that reads all orders
Only when the order is placed
items.explanation: Checking inside the method that changes state means the order is never observably invalid.

items.prompt: Can outside code edit a line item directly, skipping the order?
choices: Yes, any service may edit lines
Yes, but only during the night
No, changes go through the root
items.explanation: Direct edits would bypass the rule checks.

items.prompt: What does a repository load and save?
choices: Single line items only
Whole aggregates
Individual database columns
items.explanation: The repository is the door to storage for the entire cluster.

items.prompt: Why is there no repository for order lines?
choices: Lines are only reachable through the order root
Lines are never saved to storage by any part of the system
Lines are too small to store
items.explanation: A line repository would be a back door around the root's checks.

items.prompt: What does an invariant mean?
choices: A value that is never allowed to change after creation
A function that cannot be called twice
A rule that must hold after every change
items.explanation: Invariants are checked on every mutation, not just at the end.

items.prompt: Is an aggregate mainly a database feature or a modeling decision?
choices: A database feature you switch on
A modeling decision about what is checked together
A cloud setting for scaling
items.explanation: The database offers tools; the domain chooses the boundary.

items.prompt: `addLine` appends the line first and a separate `validate()` runs before placing. What can go wrong that checking inside `addLine` prevents?
choices: The order becomes slower because validation runs twice for every change
The order loses its identity because the line was added too early
The order is saved twice, once for the append and once for the validate
The order sits over its limit and other code can read that invalid state
items.explanation: The state is invalid between the append and the later check.
items.reference:
One door, rules checked every time
outside code calls Order.addLine only
the root checks: order still open? total + new line within limit?
the repository saves the whole Order in one call
there is no OrderLineRepository on purpose
Why: an invariant is only enforced if every change must pass through the one place that checks it.
items.learnMore:
Aggregate roots as gatekeepers

The aggregate boundary is drawn around the smallest cluster of objects that must be consistent on every write. Outside code holds a reference to the root only, so there is exactly one code path that can change the cluster.

Common mistake

Splitting validation into a separate step. Between the change and the check, the aggregate is observably invalid.
items.reflection: Pick a system you know (a bank account, a booking, a shopping cart). Which facts must always be true together, and what is the single door that should protect them?

items.prompt: An ORM lets a developer call `save()` on one `OrderLine` row. Why does that undermine the design?
choices: It makes the order slower because lines must be loaded one by one
It stores the line twice because the root also keeps a copy
It persists a change without ever running the root's rule checks
The ORM generates slower queries when lines are saved one at a time
items.explanation: The root is the only gate for invariants; a lone line save is a back door around it.

the root checks: order still open? total + new line within limit?
the repository saves the whole Order in one call
there is no OrderLineRepository on purpose

items.prompt: `Customer` is a separate aggregate that `Order` references by id only. What is the strongest reason?
choices: Customer data is too large to be loaded together with an order
Customer edits and order writes should not contend for the same consistency unit
Orders are never allowed to read anything about a customer
Customers are less likely to change their addresses while an order is open
items.explanation: The boundary encloses the smallest cluster that must be consistent on every write.

items.prompt: What makes something an entity?
choices: It is stored in a table of its own
It has an identity that persists as it changes
It is always larger than a value
items.explanation: Line 7 is still line 7 after its quantity changes.

items.prompt: What makes something a value object?
choices: It is compared by its contents, with no identity
It has a unique id column and a version number attached
It is stored forever in the database
items.explanation: Two $10 amounts are simply equal.

items.prompt: Are two separate `$10` Money objects the same object or equal?
choices: The same, because the number on each one matches
Different, because each has its own id
Equal, because only the content matters
items.explanation: Value objects have no identity to track.

items.prompt: Line 7 changes its quantity from 2 to 3. Which is true?
choices: It becomes a new line 8
It is still line 7
It stops existing as a line
items.explanation: Identity persists across changes for an entity.

items.prompt: How does a value object 'change'?
choices: You create a new value to replace it
You edit the same object in place and keep its address
You delete the whole database row
items.explanation: Value objects are immutable.

items.prompt: Which is the best fit for a value object?
choices: A customer account
An order line with an id
An amount of money
items.explanation: Money is compared by amount and currency only.

items.prompt: Which is the best fit for an entity?
choices: The number 10
An order line that can be updated by id
A color name such as 'red'
items.explanation: You need to say 'update line 7'.

items.prompt: What does an entity need that a value object does not?
choices: An identity
A longer name
A database of its own
items.explanation: Identity is what lets you say 'which one, specifically'.

items.prompt: Two order lines have identical product, quantity and unit price. Are they the same line?
choices: Yes, because all of their fields are identical
Yes, but only while the order is still open and no quantity has changed
No, they are separate lines because each has its own identity
Yes, because the product and the quantity were chosen by the same user
items.explanation: Entities with identical fields are still different things.
items.reference:
Does 'which one, exactly' matter?
entity: tracked by id, can change, stays itself (line 7)
value object: compared by contents, never edited (Money $10)
identical fields: two entities are different, two values are the same
Why: the question 'do I ever need to say which one?' decides the modeling choice.
items.learnMore:
Identity or equality?

An entity answers the question 'which one?'; a value object answers 'what is it equal to?'. Value objects are replaced rather than edited, which makes them safe to share and easy to compare.

Common mistake

Giving every object an id by habit. Identity is a cost; add it only where 'which one' matters.
items.reflection: Look at something around you, such as a coin versus a bank account number. Which parts would you track by identity and which are interchangeable?

items.prompt: A team models `Money` as an entity with an id and update methods. What does that cost them?
choices: The ability to say 'update line 7' without changing identity
Identity tracking and mutation code that nothing needs
Currency checks that only entities are able to perform
The ability to compare two amounts of money for equality
items.explanation: A value has no 'which one' question, so identity machinery is dead weight.

choices: 'Update line 7's quantity' becomes impossible, since every edit yields a different object
Two lines with the same price can no longer be added to one order, since they compare as equal and merge
The order total can no longer be calculated from its lines
The ability to give each order line its own unique id
items.explanation: Without identity, an edit cannot refer to the same line afterwards.

items.prompt: What is a domain event?
choices: A record that something important happened in the domain
A function that runs on a timer to clean up old orders
A button click in the browser
items.explanation: OrderPlaced is a fact raised by the aggregate root.

items.prompt: Who decides that OrderPlaced happened?
choices: The billing context
The user's browser
The aggregate root
items.explanation: The root checks rules and records the fact.

items.prompt: Why not call Billing's API directly from `placeOrder()`?
choices: Billing's API is always slower
It would couple the order to every downstream context
Direct calls are not allowed in any language
items.explanation: The root should not know who reacts to its events.

items.prompt: When is the event published?
choices: After the save has committed
Before the order is validated
While the root is still changing
items.explanation: Publishing after the commit means the event is only ever true.

items.prompt: What does `pullDomainEvents()` return?
choices: All orders currently stored in the database table
The current credit limit
The events recorded since the last call
items.explanation: It drains the recorded events for the application layer to publish.

items.prompt: Who publishes the recorded events?
choices: The line item that was added
The application layer after a successful save
The browser after a page reload
items.explanation: Publishing is infrastructure, not domain logic.

items.prompt: If the save fails, what happens to the recorded OrderPlaced?
choices: It is never published
It is published twice
It is sent to Billing anyway
items.explanation: The event is only published after a successful commit.

items.prompt: Which context reacts to OrderPlaced?
choices: Only the order itself, which keeps its own events private
Only the database
Any context that subscribes, such as Billing
items.explanation: The order never learns who subscribed.

items.prompt: `placeOrder()` publishes OrderPlaced the moment it is recorded, and then the save fails. What is the consequence?
choices: Billing misses the event because publishing happened too early
Billing acts on an order that was never stored
The order is stored twice because the event is replayed
Billing receives the event twice, because publishing is retried on failure
items.explanation: The event was announced before the fact was durable.
items.reference:
Record, commit, then publish
1. root checks rules, sets PLACED, records OrderPlaced
2. repository saves and commits
3. application layer publishes pullDomainEvents()
crash between 2 and 3: the outbox pattern closes that gap
Why: an event announced before the commit can describe something that never became true.
items.learnMore:
Events as true facts

A domain event is a fact raised inside one aggregate. Publishing is a separate application concern, and doing it after the commit keeps announcements truthful. For the crash-between-steps gap, an outbox stores the event with the state and publishes it later.

Common mistake

Publishing from inside the constructor or method. The save may still fail afterward.
items.reflection: Think of a news announcement or a delivery notice. What could go wrong if it were sent before the thing it announces had really happened?

items.prompt: The save commits, but the process crashes before the event is published. What problem is this?
choices: A dual-write gap: the order exists but nobody was told
A lost update: two writers overwrote each other's change
A phantom event: the bus delivered a message that never existed
A deadlock: the store and the bus each wait for the other to finish
items.explanation: Two separate systems (store and bus) were updated without one atomic step.

items.prompt: An outbox table is written in the same transaction as the aggregate. What does it trade for guaranteed delivery?
choices: Strict consistency, since events are no longer tied to saves at all
The root's invariants, since events are written outside the aggregate
Strict ordering of events, since the poller can send them in any order
Some publish latency, since a separate poller sends the events later
items.explanation: The event is durable with the state; a poller publishes it at least once, slightly later.

items.prompt: What does an anticorruption layer do?
choices: Encrypts the database at rest
Deletes old records at night
Translates another model into yours at the boundary
items.explanation: It keeps the other model's meanings out of your core.

items.prompt: What is a conformist relationship?
choices: Both teams redesign their models together as one shared model
Downstream adopts the upstream shape with no translation
The upstream always accepts requests
items.explanation: You use their shape because you have no leverage.

items.prompt: When does customer-supplier fit?
choices: Both teams are in one organization and can negotiate
The supplier is a third-party vendor with its own roadmap
There is only one team in total
items.explanation: The downstream's needs can feed the upstream's plans.

items.prompt: What is a published language?
choices: A programming language only used in docs
A spoken language used in meetings
One stable, versioned contract shared with many consumers
items.explanation: It replaces many custom integrations with one contract.

items.prompt: A third-party API you cannot change is best modeled as which relationship?
choices: Customer-supplier, with a negotiated roadmap between the teams
Conformist, often behind an anticorruption layer
Shared kernel
items.explanation: You have no leverage, so you adapt rather than negotiate.

items.prompt: Is a context boundary only a drawing on a whiteboard?
choices: No, it shows up as modules, services and deployments
Yes, it never affects code and only appears in diagrams
Yes, until the system is large
items.explanation: The boundary is enforced by where code lives and what it exposes.

items.prompt: Many downstream teams need the same upstream data. Which pattern fits?
choices: A private integration for each team
A shared database table
Open host service with a published language
items.explanation: One stable contract beats many bespoke ones.

items.prompt: Why name the relationship instead of saying 'it is an API'?
choices: APIs are always conformist, so the label adds nothing new to know
Each relationship implies a different way of handling change
Names make code run faster
items.explanation: The label tells you whether to translate, negotiate or conform.

items.prompt: A team keeps filing feature requests with a payment vendor that has never changed its API for anyone. Which relationship was misread?
choices: A conformist edge was treated like customer-supplier
A customer-supplier edge was treated like conformist
A published language was treated like an anticorruption layer
A published language was treated as an anticorruption layer
items.explanation: With no leverage, you adapt; requests will not be heard.
items.reference:
Which relationship is this edge?
no leverage over upstream: conformist (+ anticorruption layer if the model is foreign)
same organization, can negotiate: customer-supplier
many consumers, one dataset: open host service / published language
foreign meanings to keep out: anticorruption layer
Why: each pattern decides who adapts, and misreading it wastes effort or absorbs avoidable change.
items.learnMore:
From context map to code

A context boundary becomes a module, a repository, a service and a deployment unit over time. The relationship pattern tells you who changes when something changes: you translate, you conform, you negotiate, or you consume a stable published contract.

Common mistake

Calling every connection 'an API'. The label hides whether you have leverage and who must adapt.
items.reflection: Think of two groups you work with, such as a vendor and a neighbouring team. Do you adapt to them, negotiate with them, or use a shared contract?

items.prompt: Two teams in one company depend on each other's roadmaps, yet the downstream team silently absorbs every breaking change. What was missed?
choices: It should have built an anticorruption layer, because the upstream is third-party
It should have published a language, because it has many consumers
It should have become a conformist to the other team's schedule
It had standing to negotiate as a customer, but behaved as a conformist
items.explanation: Within one organization the downstream can ask; silent absorption wastes that leverage.

In the browser, so the legacy shape stays out of every server
In an adapter at the boundary, so the Order model never sees the legacy shape

items.prompt: What does optimistic concurrency assume?
choices: Conflicts always happen, so every write must take a lock first
Conflicts are rare, so detect them at save time
Conflicts cannot be detected at all
items.explanation: It does not lock up front; it checks when saving.

items.prompt: What does the repository compare on save?
choices: The version the writer loaded and the version stored now
The writer's name and the exact time the request was received
The order total and the credit limit
items.explanation: A mismatch means someone saved in between.

items.prompt: Request B saves with version 1 but the store is at version 2. What happens?
choices: The save overwrites version 2
The save is merged automatically
The save is rejected as a conflict
items.explanation: B's copy is out of date.

items.prompt: After a conflict, what should B do?
choices: Retry the same object again, unchanged, until it works
Reload the current order and try again
Ignore the error and move on
items.explanation: The retry must start from fresh data.

items.prompt: Who checks that total stays within the limit?
choices: The aggregate root
The repository's version number
The database's disk
items.explanation: Validity is the root's job; freshness is the repository's.

items.prompt: Why is the conflict better than the original bug?
choices: It never happens at all
It makes both writes succeed
It is visible instead of silent
items.explanation: Exactly one of two conflicting writes succeeds, and the other is told.

items.prompt: Retrying `save` with the same stale object will do what?
choices: Succeed the second time
Conflict again
Merge with the newer data
items.explanation: The object still carries the old version.

items.prompt: If more writes target one aggregate, the chance of a conflict does what?
choices: It goes up
It goes down
It stays exactly the same
items.explanation: More competing writes make an overlap more likely.

items.prompt: At 2 writes per second to one order and a 150 ms write window, the chance of a competing write is about 26%. What does that tell you?
choices: Conflicts are so rare that version checks are not worth the effort
Conflicts are certain, so every save should take a lock first
Conflicts are rare enough that a version check is not worth adding
Conflicts are routine at that load, so retries must be designed in
items.explanation: About one in four writes meets a competitor, so conflict handling is part of normal operation.
items.reference:
What the repository compares
A loads v1, B loads v1
A saves with base v1: stored as v2
B saves with base v1, store is v2: conflict
B reloads v2 (total $95), adds $12: root rejects $107
Why: validity is checked by the root; freshness of the starting snapshot is checked by the version.
items.learnMore:
Optimistic concurrency

Instead of locking, every stored aggregate carries a version. A save must present the version it loaded, otherwise it is refused. The caller reloads the current state and re-runs the business rule, which is where stale assumptions get caught.

Common mistake

Retrying with the same loaded object. It still holds the old version and the old data, so it conflicts forever.
items.reflection: Think of booking the last seat on a shared calendar. What should you do when told someone else changed it while you were deciding?

items.prompt: Request B hits a conflict and reloads. The reloaded total is $95 and B adds $12. What happens?
choices: The repository merges the lines, so the order is stored at $107
The root accepts it, since B's earlier $92 check already passed
The root rejects the line, since $107 is over the $100 limit
The repository merges both lines and saves the order at $107
items.explanation: The retry runs the rule against the real total, which catches what the stale copy hid.

items.prompt: Which change lowers the conflict chance in the formula 1 - exp(-rate × window)?
choices: Longer transactions, so each write carries more validation work and holds its version longer
A narrower aggregate, so fewer writes target each version number
More retries per request, so conflicts are resolved faster
A longer retry delay, so that the competing write has time to finish
items.explanation: The rate falls when traffic is spread over smaller aggregates; shorter windows also help.

items.prompt: What is a risk of a very large aggregate?
choices: Unrelated writes contend for the same version
It cannot be stored in one table of a database
It has no root
items.explanation: Everything inside shares one consistency unit.

items.prompt: What is a risk of a very small aggregate?
choices: It cannot be named, so teams cannot talk about it clearly in design reviews
It uses too much disk
A rule that spans several aggregates cannot be checked atomically
items.explanation: The rule spans separate saves.

items.prompt: Which is the better guide for the boundary?
choices: Everything one feature touches
The smallest cluster that must be consistent on every write
Whatever fits in one file
items.explanation: Size follows the rules, not the feature.

items.prompt: If `OrderLine` were its own aggregate, which rule loses its owner?
choices: The total-at-most-limit rule
The line's own quantity must be positive
The product has a name
items.explanation: The total depends on all lines.

items.prompt: Why is `Customer` kept out of `Order`?
choices: Because customers never exist anywhere inside an order system
Because orders have no owner
To avoid unrelated edits contending with order writes
items.explanation: They have different rules and traffic.

items.prompt: What can coordinate a rule across aggregates?
choices: A bigger font in the UI
A saga or a compensating step
A second copy of the data
items.explanation: It trades strict consistency for availability.

items.prompt: Smaller aggregates usually lead to what about conflicts?
choices: Fewer of them
More of them
No change at all
items.explanation: Write traffic is spread over more version numbers.

items.prompt: Is stricter consistency always the goal?
choices: Yes, always, whatever the cost to throughput
Yes, when the system is small
No, it costs contention and throughput
items.explanation: The boundary is a trade-off.

items.prompt: An order aggregate also contains the customer's address book. Many customer edits now delay order placement. What is the best fix?
choices: Add more retries with a longer back-off to the order save so that conflicts clear up
Lock the address book longer so that orders wait their turn
Move the customer data into its own aggregate, referenced by id
Make the order aggregate hold the whole customer record as well
items.explanation: The customer's edits and the order's rules do not need to be consistent together.
items.reference:
Boundary trade-offs
too large: unrelated writes share one version, contention rises
too small: a rule spanning aggregates needs a saga
right size: the smallest cluster that must be consistent on every write
reference other aggregates by id; pass values in
Why: the boundary that guarantees consistency also serializes writers.
items.learnMore:
Sizing an aggregate

Ask which rules must be true at the instant of every write, and enclose only the objects those rules mention. Everything else can be referenced by id and kept consistent eventually through events or a saga.

Common mistake

Putting in everything a feature touches. The boundary should follow the rules, not the screen.
items.reflection: Think of a team that shares one big task list. Which items truly must be updated together, and which could be separate lists that sync later?

items.prompt: Each order line becomes its own aggregate and the total-at-most-limit rule still has to hold. What does that now require?
choices: A faster database so that all line saves finish together
A coordinating process that checks and compensates after the fact
A version number on each line so that conflicts become impossible
Merge all lines into one value object that is replaced on every edit
items.explanation: No single save can see all lines, so the rule needs a saga or a compensating step.

choices: Does the order aggregate hold more than the rules need, or is it split poorly?
Which retry delay will make the conflicts disappear for good?
Which database isolation level will stop version checks from failing?
Which isolation level lets a hot order save without any conflict?
items.explanation: At that load the boundary, not the retry policy, is the lever (about 99.8% at a 150 ms window).
